claims.text: The raw repository source explicitly records a coding question asking for zigzag printing/traversal of a binary tree, so a zigzag level-order traversal contract is directly supported rather than inferred from an unrelated template.

LeetCode 103 defines zigzag level order as left-to-right on one level, right-to-left on the next, alternating thereafter; standard examples include [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] -> [[3],[20,9],[15,7]], [1] -> [[1]], and [] -> [].

Freezing queue.size() at the start of each BFS level isolates exactly that depth; writing each dequeued value to index i or levelSize-1-i changes only output order while keeping child enqueue order stable for the next depth.

The BFS implementation enqueues and dequeues every node once, so runtime is O(n); the queue and current-level/result storage can be linear in the number of nodes in the widest level, giving O(n) worst-case auxiliary storage.

The exact self-contained Java implementation passes empty/single/standard examples, complete and skewed trees, duplicate values, and 3000 deterministic random trees compared with an independent DFS-by-depth oracle.

checks: 3000 deterministic random trees compared against DFS-by-depth oracle

findings: The repository source explicitly asks for zigzag binary-tree printing, so the candidate does not rely on the old generic tree template for its core contract.
The public LeetCode 103 contract and examples match the repository question's expected output shape and alternating level order.
The implementation separates BFS visitation order from zigzag output order, which keeps the next-level queue invariant simple and avoids double-reversal mistakes.
The index mapping is one-to-one within a frozen level and preserves every node exactly once.

The candidate code fence now includes all java.util imports and is byte-for-byte equivalent in implementation body to the repository validation fixture, so the shared standalone javac audit and the differential fixture validate the same solution.
The self-contained Java candidate compiles standalone, while the repository fixture passes targeted boundaries and 3000 deterministic random comparisons against a structurally different DFS oracle.
No project or interview experience is fabricated; required human approval remains a separate promotion gate.
